items.addition: This addition looks like a plain block box. But inside every wall there's a hidden steel cage, built for hurricanes. Here's what's behind it. It starts in the ground. We dig the footing and tie the rebar, because concrete is strong when you squeeze it, but weak when you pull it. Steel takes the pull. Then the block goes up. See those bars sticking out of the footing? Every few feet, a bar runs up through a hollow block cell, and we fill that cell with concrete. That's a tie column. Tip: ask your contractor to show you where they are on your plans. On top, we form and pour a tie beam. It wraps the whole room like a belt and locks every column together. Then the roof. Each truss gets a metal connector, so the wind can't lift the roof off the walls. Roof to connectors, connectors to tie beam, tie beam to columns, columns to footing. That's a continuous load path. In Broward and Miami-Dade, it's built to High Velocity Hurricane Zone rules, some of the toughest in the country. Planning an addition in South Florida? Let's build it right.
items.front: Nineteen days. Zero walls. And this is the most important part of the whole addition. Day one, we clear the landscaping and mark the footprint. Then the excavator digs the footings, the strip of concrete the whole addition stands on. South Florida soil is sandy, so it has to be compacted, or the slab settles and cracks later. Next come the forms and the rebar. The steel sits up on supports so it ends up wrapped in concrete, never touching the dirt, so it can't rust. Then the part you'll never see again: plumbing. Every drain under the new floor goes in now, and gets inspected before any concrete is poured. Before the slab, Florida code requires termite protection. The soil is treated, then covered with a vapor barrier. And then, finally, the first block goes down. Week three, and the walls are rising. Follow along, the tie beam is next.
